doc.title: Frank Tate interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001

title: Bad gigs, Buddy Rich's rant and Zoot's compliment
summary: Tate reflects on temperamental leaders and encouragement, citing Buddy Rich, Zoot Sims and Bobby Short.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: this band. And so we’re known going in so there’s none of this hey you guys go through the kitchen. Most of the gigs I play I’m part of the party, if I want to be, and so I don’t have that problem much anymore. And there were some gigs that I’ve been on that were misery but it’s only four hours a night max and it’s over. How bad can it be? And all gigs end. I mean it’s two weeks, three weeks somewhere and it’s over. I’ve had some problems with some temperamental people and things, and they can really get underneath your skin. And it’s too bad because I’ve seen really, really fine musicians wreck gigs. Guys that ought to known better. I say guys, people. Singers, men, women that ought to know better and ought to understand the psychology of what makes a band work well. You don’t start a fight with somebody in your band. Buddy Rich used to, like there’s a tape floating around of him railing on the band. These are a bunch of 20 year olds that he robbed out of Berklee, and they’re great players all, and he just attacked them on the bus one night. And I had been hearing about this tape and I was all excited, I wanted to hear it, and I listened to like three seconds of it and I said I don’t know what this is but it’s not fun. It can’t be fun for these guys, and it was really embarrassing. And all he had to do, because they all revered him, he was like such a superior player, all he had to do was say, “Yeah guys, that was just fantastic tonight” and they would have been even better the next night. They were all like 20 and 21, very impressionable, and that’s not even an age thing. I mean compliments to a guy that’s playing can really change the whole — I worked with, one night when I was working with Zoot we had been to Belfast and I had played on a strange bass. It’s now a bass that I own, I bought it from the guy. But it was really big and difficult for me to play at the time. It had a big string length and it was very wide. And Zoot commented at the time, he says, “You’ve got some intonation troubles there.” And I said, “Well Zoot, I’m using a borrowed bass.” He says, “Yeah I guess you are.” And then a couple of weeks later, in Chicago, I was back on my own instrument at the time and we had been playing steadily. And he laid a compliment on me that stuck with me to this day, and I mean I walked down, got off the elevator and walked down to my room three feet off the floor. And I was in my mid-30s then. You know, it wasn’t child psychology he was using on me. So I just, why wreck a gig. You know his comment about the intonation was well taken, he wasn’t trying to start a fight with me, but he had some tapes of it and he said, “Hey you know, this is something you need to look into.” And I did. It made me think about it more. But he never went on a rant. Bobby never does either. Bobby can get angry, everybody can. He gets angry and then he gets over it and gets on with the next piece of business. If something bothers him he’ll let you know, that’s the end of it. He’s very fair like that and he makes it clear that he’s forgotten about it after it’s over and it doesn’t happen but once in a blue moon anyhow.
